claim: AKT is a serine-threonine kinase that regulates proliferation and survival by phosphorylating a network of protein substrates.
source: The serine–threonine kinase AKT regulates proliferation and survival by phosphorylating a network of protein substrates.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about AKT function.

claim: Catalytically inactive AKT (K179M) protected cancer cells from drug-induced cell death in a PH-domain dependent manner in cells with gain-of-function alterations in MET, HER2, or PI3K.
source: In cancer cells harboring gain-of-function alterations in MET, HER2, or Phosphatidyl-Inositol-3-Kinase (PI3K), catalytically inactive AKT (K179M) protected from drug induced cell death in a PH-domain dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the results section.

claim: The AKT kinase domain mutant G161V found in human melanoma lacked enzymatic activity in vitro and in AKT1/AKT2 double knockout cells.
source: An AKT kinase domain mutant found in human melanoma (G161V) lacked enzymatic activity in vitro and in AKT1/AKT2 double knockout cells, but promoted growth factor independent survival of primary human melanocytes.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assays and Western blot data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: The AKT G161V mutant promoted growth factor independent survival of primary human melanocytes.
source: An AKT kinase domain mutant found in human melanoma (G161V) lacked enzymatic activity in vitro and in AKT1/AKT2 double knockout cells, but promoted growth factor independent survival of primary human melanocytes.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors failed to block the kinase-independent function of AKT.
source: ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors failed to block the kinase-independent function of AKT, a liability that limits their effectiveness compared to allosteric AKT inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assays comparing MK2206 with GSK690693 and GDC0068 shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The inability of ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors to block kinase-independent AKT function is a liability that limits their effectiveness compared to allosteric AKT inhibitors.
source: ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors failed to block the kinase-independent function of AKT, a liability that limits their effectiveness compared to allosteric AKT inhibitors.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data comparing the two classes of inhibitors.

claim: AKT is aberrantly activated in many human cancers, usually due to mutations in upstream components of the PI3K pathway.
source: AKT is aberrantly activated in many human cancers, usually due to mutations in upstream components of the Phosphatidyl-Inositol-3-Kinase (PI3K) pathway.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: AKT signaling is required for tumor maintenance in cancer cell lines harboring PI3K mutations or amplification of the HER2 receptor tyrosine kinase.
source: AKT signaling is required for tumor maintenance in certain genetic contexts, as has been shown for some cancer cell lines harboring PI3K mutations or amplification of the HER2 receptor tyrosine kinase (She et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to She et al., 2008.

claim: The allosteric AKT inhibitor MK2206 induced significantly more cell death than ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors GSK690693 and GDC0068 in EBC1 cells.
source: When we compared the ability of the AKT inhibitors to induce cell death using a trypan blue exclusion assay, we observed significantly greater cell death induction by the allosteric inhibitor MK2206 compared to the ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors GSK690693 (Figure 1B—source data 1) and GDC0068 (Figure 1C—source data 1) despite less complete inhibition of AKT substrate phosphorylation at these drug concentrations (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by trypan blue exclusion assay data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: MK2206 induced significantly greater cell death than GSK690693 despite less complete inhibition of AKT substrate phosphorylation at the tested drug concentrations.
source: When we compared the ability of the AKT inhibitors to induce cell death using a trypan blue exclusion assay, we observed significantly greater cell death induction by the allosteric inhibitor MK2206 compared to the ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors GSK690693 (Figure 1B—source data 1) and GDC0068 (Figure 1C—source data 1) despite less complete inhibition of AKT substrate phosphorylation at these drug concentrations (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1A showing substrate phosphorylation and cell death data in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors induced hyper-phosphorylation of AKT at threonine 308 and serine 473.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Okuzumi et al., 2009), the ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors induced hyper-phosphorylation of AKT at the two regulatory phosphorylation sites threonine 308 and serine 473.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1A and is consistent with cited literature (Okuzumi et al., 2009).

claim: EBC1 cells harbor amplification of MET, a receptor tyrosine kinase that mediates critical oncogenic signals through the PI3K/AKT axis.
source: We had selected EBC1 lung cancer cells for our initial studies because they harbor amplification of MET, a receptor tyrosine kinase that mediates critical oncogenic signals through the PI3K/AKT axis (Gherardi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for cell line selection and is supported by a citation to Gherardi et al., 2012.

claim: MK2206 induced significantly more cell death than GSK690693 in MET-amplified H1993, H1648 NSCLC cell lines and GTL-16 gastric cancer cells.
source: To test whether other MET-amplified human cancer cells show a similar drug response pattern, we extended our experiments to MET-amplified H1993 and H1648 NSCLC cell lines and GTL-16 gastric cancer cells. MK2206 again induced significantly more cell death than GSK690693 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: MK2206 induced significantly more cell death than ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors in breast cancer cell lines with HER2 amplification and/or PIK3CA-mutation.
source: In cell lines with other PI3K pathway alterations previously associated with 'AKT-dependence' (She et al., 2008), we also found that MK2006 induced significantly more cell death than ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors. These cell lines included breast cancer cells with HER2 amplification and/or PIK3CA-mutation (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: MK2206 did not induce cell death in non-transformed bronchial epithelial cells.
source: In contrast, MK2206 did not induce cell death in non-transformed bronchial epithelial cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation but data is not shown.

claim: MK2206 did not induce cell death in lung cancer cell lines with activating EGFR mutations.
source: MK2206 also did not induce cell death in lung cancer cell lines with activating EGFR mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Figure 1—source data 1) which have been linked with aberrant PI3K pathway activation (Engelman et al., 2005), suggesting that the mode of PI3K activation is critical in establishing AKT addiction in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The mode of PI3K activation is critical in establishing AKT addiction in cancer.
source: MK2206 also did not induce cell death in lung cancer cell lines with activating EGFR mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Figure 1—source data 1) which have been linked with aberrant PI3K pathway activation (Engelman et al., 2005), suggesting that the mode of PI3K activation is critical in establishing AKT addiction in cancer.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential response of cell lines with different PI3K pathway alterations.

claim: Expression of AKT1 W80A or AKT2 W80A completely rescued MK2206-induced cell death.
source: Expression of AKT1 W80A or AKT2 W80A but not wild-type AKT1 or wild-type AKT2 completely rescued MK2206-induced cell death (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Wild-type AKT1 or wild-type AKT2 did not rescue MK2206-induced cell death.
source: Expression of AKT1 W80A or AKT2 W80A but not wild-type AKT1 or wild-type AKT2 completely rescued MK2206-induced cell death (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: AKT1 W80A and AKT2 W80A alleles are biochemically insensitive to MK2206.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed that these AKT alleles are biochemically insensitive to MK2206 and prevented the induction of PARP cleavage, a marker of apoptosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 6, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: AKT1 W80A and AKT2 W80A prevented the induction of PARP cleavage, a marker of apoptosis.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed that these AKT alleles are biochemically insensitive to MK2206 and prevented the induction of PARP cleavage, a marker of apoptosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 6, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing PARP cleavage in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: All three AKT inhibitors (MK2206, GSK690693, and GDC0068) were able to induce near-complete proliferation arrest.
source: Of note, all three inhibitors were able to induce near-complete proliferation arrest (Figure 1—figure supplement 7, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Allosteric and ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors differ in their ability to block AKT-mediated survival.
source: These results demonstrate that allosteric and ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors differ in their ability to block AKT-mediated survival, and that this survival signal can be mediated by AKT1 or AKT2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing the two classes of inhibitors.

claim: The AKT-mediated survival signal can be mediated by AKT1 or AKT2.
source: These results demonstrate that allosteric and ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors differ in their ability to block AKT-mediated survival, and that this survival signal can be mediated by AKT1 or AKT2.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that both AKT1 W80A and AKT2 W80A can rescue MK2206-induced cell death.

claim: AKT regulates survival through phosphorylation of several protein substrates.
source: AKT regulates survival through phosphorylation of several protein substrates.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about AKT function.

claim: GSK690693 antagonized the ability of crizotinib to kill EBC1 cells despite inducing a modest amount of cell death as single agent.
source: Despite inducing a modest amount of cell death as single agent, GSK690693 antagonized the ability of crizotinib to kill EBC1 cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The allosteric AKT inhibitor MK2206 did not compromise the ability of crizotinib to induce cell death.
source: The allosteric AKT inhibitor MK2206, in contrast, did not compromise the ability of crizotinib to induce cell death (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Catalytically inactive AKT1-K179M protected MCF7, MDA-MB-361, and EBC1 cells from MK2206-induced cell death.
source: When we expressed this mutant in MCF7 breast cancer cells, MDA-MB-361 breast cancer cells and EBC1 lung cancer cells, catalytically inactive AKT (Figure 2C/D/E, Figure 2—source data 1) but not wild-type AKT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1), protected from MK2206-induced cell death.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figures 2C, 2D, and 2E.

claim: Wild-type AKT did not protect from MK2206-induced cell death.
source: When we expressed this mutant in MCF7 breast cancer cells, MDA-MB-361 breast cancer cells and EBC1 lung cancer cells, catalytically inactive AKT (Figure 2C/D/E, Figure 2—source data 1) but not wild-type AKT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1), protected from MK2206-induced cell death.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The protection by the K179M-AKT allele was only partial, consistent with the coexistence of kinase-independent and kinase-dependent AKT signals.
source: Compared to the complete cell death protection provided by the drug-resistant W80A-AKT allele (Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 1), the protection by the K179M-AKT allele was only partial, consistent with the coexistence of kinase-independent and kinase-dependent AKT signals.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing the degree of protection provided by different AKT mutants.

claim: Catalytically inactive AKT protected from cell death following doxycycline treatment and AKT depletion in EBC1 cells.
source: Similar to our results with pharmacological AKT blockade, catalytically inactive AKT protected from cell death following doxycycline treatment and AKT depletion of these cells (Figure 2F, bottom, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: MK2206 markedly impaired phosphoinositide binding of AKT.
source: Using a PI pull-down assay, we observed that MK2206 markedly impaired phosphoinositide binding (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by PIP-binding assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Allosteric AKT inhibitors lock AKT in a closed conformation with its phospholipid binding site blocked by the kinase domain.
source: This result is consistent with findings from structural studies that allosteric AKT inhibitors lock AKT in a closed conformation with its phospholipid binding site blocked by the kinase domain (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to structural studies by Wu et al., 2010.

claim: Incubation with the ATP-competitive inhibitor GSK690693 increased binding of AKT to PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns(3,4,5)P3.
source: In contrast to our findings with MK2206, incubation with the ATP-competitive inhibitor GSK690693 increased binding of AKT to PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns (3,4,5)P3 and this was associated with increased localization of AKT to the plasma membrane (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by PIP-binding assay data shown in Figure 3A and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B.

claim: GSK690693 treatment was associated with increased localization of AKT to the plasma membrane.
source: In contrast to our findings with MK2206, incubation with the ATP-competitive inhibitor GSK690693 increased binding of AKT to PtdIns(3,4)P2 and PtdIns (3,4,5)P3 and this was associated with increased localization of AKT to the plasma membrane (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The AKT1-K179M mutant was hyper-phosphorylated at T308.
source: Similar to GSK690693-bound AKT, the AKT1-K179M (or AKT2-K181M) mutant was hyper-phosphorylated at T308 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kinase-dead AKT was constitutively localized to the plasma membrane in MCF10A and EBC1 cells.
source: This phosphorylation event occurs at the plasma membrane (Stephens et al., 1998) and immunofluorescence in MCF10A and EBC1 cells confirmed that kinase-dead AKT was constitutively localized to the plasma membrane (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A myristoylated ΔPH-AKT1-K179M mutant was unable to inhibit MK2206-induced cell death.
source: To examine whether membrane localization was sufficient for the pro-survival function of AKT1-K179M, we replaced the PH-domain of AKT1-K179M by a membrane-targeting myristoylation signal and expressed this mutant in EBC1 cells. This mutant was unable to inhibit MK2206-induced cell death (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1) despite being constitutively phosphorylated in the presence of MK2206 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The myristoylated ΔPH-AKT1-K179M mutant was constitutively phosphorylated in the presence of MK2206.
source: To examine whether membrane localization was sufficient for the pro-survival function of AKT1-K179M, we replaced the PH-domain of AKT1-K179M by a membrane-targeting myristoylation signal and expressed this mutant in EBC1 cells. This mutant was unable to inhibit MK2206-induced cell death (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1) despite being constitutively phosphorylated in the presence of MK2206 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The R86A/K179M double mutant showed loss of AKT phosphorylation at threonine 308 when expressed in HCT116 cells that express no endogenous AKT.
source: Consistent with a loss of membrane localization, the R86A/K179M double mutant showed loss of AKT phosphorylation at threonine 308 when expressed in HCT116 cells that express no endogenous AKT (Ericson et al., 2010) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) and it did not protect from MK2206-induced dephosphorylation in cells which do express endogenous AKT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Abrogation of phosphoinositide binding by the R86A substitution did not impair the pro-survival function of kinase-defective AKT.
source: Abrogation of phosphoinositide binding by the R86A substitution did not impair the pro-survival function of kinase-defective AKT (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A second mutation (R25C) known to abolish phosphoinositide binding did not impair the pro-survival function of kinase-defective AKT.
source: We observed a similar result with a second mutation (R25C) known to abolish phosphoinositide binding (Thomas et al., 2002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Five AKT2 kinase domain mutations occurred in at least two independent cancer samples: G161V/E, R170W, I289M, H355Y, R368C/H.
source: Our survey of published cancer sequencing data identified five AKT2 kinase domain mutations that occurred in at least two independent samples (G161V/E, R170W, I289M, H355Y, R368C/H) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on a survey of published cancer sequencing data.

claim: AKT2-G161V showed complete loss of in vitro AKT substrate phosphorylation, comparable to the synthetic kinase-dead K181M-AKT2 mutant.
source: AKT2-G161V, but none of the other four kinase domain mutants, showed complete loss of in vitro AKT substrate phosphorylation, comparable to the synthetic kinase-dead K181M-AKT2 mutant included as control in our experiments (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Whole-cell lysates from G161V-AKT2 expressing cells showed loss of phosphorylation for the endogenous AKT kinase substrates PRAS40 and BAD.
source: Whole-cell lysates from G161V-AKT2 expressing cells showed loss of phosphorylation for the endogenous AKT kinase substrates PRAS40 and BAD (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: AKT2-G161V showed altered phosphoinositide binding with acquired preference for PtdIns(4,5)P2, similar to the synthetic kinase-dead AKT2 mutant.
source: In the phosphoinositide pull-down assay, AKT2-G161V showed altered phosphoinositide binding with acquired preference for PtdIns(4,5)P2, again similar to the synthetic kinase-dead AKT2 mutant (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by PIP-binding assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Immortalized human melanocytes acquired the ability to survive in TPA-deficient media after stable expression of AKT2-G161V.
source: These cells required 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate (TPA) for survival in culture, as has previously been reported (Arita et al., 1992), but acquired the ability to survive in TPA-deficient media (RPMI) after stable expression of AKT2-G161V (Figure 4E, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The E17K-AKT1 mutant localizes to the plasma membrane due to increased affinity for the constitutive plasma membrane lipid PI(4,5)P2.
source: The increased PI(4,5)P2 binding of the kinase-dead G161V-AKT2 mutant (Figure 4D) was reminiscent of the most common somatic AKT mutation in human cancer (E17K-AKT1) which localizes to the plasma membrane due to increased affinity for the constitutive plasma membrane lipid PI(4,5)P2 (Carpten et al., 2007; Landgraf et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carpten et al., 2007 and Landgraf et al., 2008.

claim: Cells transduced with the E17K-AKT1 mutant showed residual AKT phosphorylation at equimolar concentrations of MK2206.
source: Compared to cells transduced with wild-type AKT, cells transduced with the E17K-AKT1 mutant showed residual AKT phosphorylation at equimolar concentrations of MK2206 (Figure 4F), consistent with the reported reduced sensitivity of E17K-AKT1 to allosteric ATP kinase inhibitors (Calleja et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2010; Parikh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Expression of E17K-AKT1 provided partial protection from MK2206-induced cell death.
source: Expression of E17K-AKT1 provided partial protection from MK2206-induced cell death (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The E17K/K179M-AKT1 double mutant provided a similar degree of protection as the E17K-AKT1 single mutant.
source: Interestingly, the E17K/K179M-AKT1 double mutant provided a similar degree of protection as the E17K-AKT1 single mutant, suggesting that this cancer-associated PH-domain mutant can mediate survival signals independent of its catalytic activity in certain cellular contexts.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The E17K-AKT1 PH-domain mutant can mediate survival signals independent of its catalytic activity in certain cellular contexts.
source: Interestingly, the E17K/K179M-AKT1 double mutant provided a similar degree of protection as the E17K-AKT1 single mutant, suggesting that this cancer-associated PH-domain mutant can mediate survival signals independent of its catalytic activity in certain cellular contexts.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that the kinase-dead E17K/K179M double mutant provides similar protection as the E17K single mutant.

claim: AKT1-G311D failed to induce phosphorylation of endogenous AKT substrates in AKT1/2 DKO HCT116 cells.
source: Lastly, we identified a human endometrial cancer cell line with a kinase domain mutation in AKT1 (G311D) (Barretina et al., 2012) that failed to induce phosphorylation of endogenous AKT substrates in AKT1/2 DKO HCT116 cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous AKT1 resulted in substantially greater cell death induction than knockdown of AKT2 in MFE-319 endometrial cancer cells.
source: While knockdown of endogenous AKT1 or AKT2 resulted in growth inhibition, knockdown of AKT1 resulted in substantially greater cell death induction than knockdown of AKT2 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting a state of addiction to signals provided by the mutant AKT1.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MFE-319 endometrial cancer cells show a state of addiction to signals provided by the mutant AKT1-G311D.
source: While knockdown of endogenous AKT1 or AKT2 resulted in growth inhibition, knockdown of AKT1 resulted in substantially greater cell death induction than knockdown of AKT2 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting a state of addiction to signals provided by the mutant AKT1.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the differential effects of AKT1 vs AKT2 knockdown.

claim: This work represents the first example of a kinase-independent function of AKT.
source: The work presented here represents the first example of a kinase-independent function of AKT (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion section.

claim: Catalytically inactivating kinase domain mutations (AKT1-K179M, AKT2-K181M, AKT2-G161V) or ATP-competitive inhibitor binding to wild-type AKT can promote phosphoinositide binding.
source: Our findings that catalytically inactivating kinase domain mutations (AKT1-K179M, AKT2-K181M, AKT2-G161V) or ATP-competitive inhibitor binding to wild-type AKT can promote phosphoinositide binding document the critical importance of the kinase domain conformation on AKT PH-domain functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the PIP-binding assay data presented in the results.

claim: The kinase domain conformation is critically important for AKT PH-domain functions.
source: Our findings that catalytically inactivating kinase domain mutations (AKT1-K179M, AKT2-K181M, AKT2-G161V) or ATP-competitive inhibitor binding to wild-type AKT can promote phosphoinositide binding document the critical importance of the kinase domain conformation on AKT PH-domain functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing how kinase domain mutations affect PH-domain function.

claim: Hyper-phosphorylation of AKT in response to ATP-competitive inhibitors may be due to increased phosphorylation at the plasma membrane in addition to impaired phosphatase access.
source: It also suggests that hyper-phosphorylation of AKT in response to ATP-competitive inhibitors (Okuzumi et al., 2009) may not only be due to impaired phosphatase access (Chan et al., 2011) but also due to increased phosphorylation at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that ATP-competitive inhibitors increase membrane localization and phosphorylation of AKT.

claim: The loss of phosphoinositide binding does not completely abolish the pro-survival function of kinase-deficient AKT.
source: Furthermore, given that the loss of phosphoinositide binding does not completely abolish the pro-survival function of kinase-deficient AKT, we suspect that the PH-domain promotes cell survival through regulation of interacting protein partners, and that perturbations in the kinase domain can influence PH-domain function by altering the ability of AKT to reach the appropriate sub-cellular compartment (likely those richest in PI(4,5)P2) and/or interact with specific effector proteins.
evidence: This is based on the observation that R86A and R25C mutations, which abolish phosphoinositide binding, do not completely eliminate the pro-survival function.

claim: The PH-domain promotes cell survival through regulation of interacting protein partners.
source: Furthermore, given that the loss of phosphoinositide binding does not completely abolish the pro-survival function of kinase-deficient AKT, we suspect that the PH-domain promotes cell survival through regulation of interacting protein partners, and that perturbations in the kinase domain can influence PH-domain function by altering the ability of AKT to reach the appropriate sub-cellular compartment (likely those richest in PI(4,5)P2) and/or interact with specific effector proteins.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: Perturbations in the kinase domain can influence PH-domain function by altering the ability of AKT to reach the appropriate sub-cellular compartment and/or interact with specific effector proteins.
source: Furthermore, given that the loss of phosphoinositide binding does not completely abolish the pro-survival function of kinase-deficient AKT, we suspect that the PH-domain promotes cell survival through regulation of interacting protein partners, and that perturbations in the kinase domain can influence PH-domain function by altering the ability of AKT to reach the appropriate sub-cellular compartment (likely those richest in PI(4,5)P2) and/or interact with specific effector proteins.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: Cancer-associated AKT mutations that favor an open conformation show reduced sensitivity to allosteric AKT inhibitors but retain sensitivity to ATP-competitive inhibitors.
source: Previous studies have shown that cancer-associated AKT mutations that favor an open conformation show reduced sensitivity to allosteric AKT inhibitors but retain sensitivity to ATP-competitive inhibitors (Calleja et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2010; Parikh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cancer cells with aberrant AKT activation by common PI3K pathway lesions (HER2, PIK3CA, MET) show reduced sensitivity to ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors.
source: Here, we show that cancer cells with aberrant AKT activation by common PI3K pathway lesions (HER2, PIK3CA, MET) show the opposite drug sensitivity profile with reduced sensitivity to ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing allosteric and ATP-competitive inhibitors.

claim: The inability of ATP-competitive inhibitors to suppress non-catalytic AKT functions in certain genetic contexts may represent a liability compared to allosteric AKT inhibitors.
source: The inability of ATP-competitive inhibitors to suppress non-catalytic AKT functions in certain genetic contexts may represent a liability compared to allosteric AKT inhibitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: EBC1 cells were obtained from the Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources (JCRB) Cell Bank.
source: EBC1 cells were obtained from the Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources (JCRB) Cell Bank.
evidence: This is a statement about the source of materials used in the study.

claim: HCT116 AKT1−/− AKT2 −/− cells were kindly provided by Dr Bert Vogelstein.
source: HCT116 AKT1−/− AKT2 −/− (HCT116-DKO) cells were kindly provided by Dr Bert Vogelstein (Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine).
evidence: This is a statement about the source of materials used in the study.

claim: In the absence of growth factors, AKT is inactive because intermolecular interactions between the pleckstrin homology (PH) and kinase domain (KD) keep the kinase in a closed conformation.
source: In the absence of growth factors, AKT is inactive because intermolecular interactions between the pleckstrin homology (PH) and kinase domain (KD) keep the kinase in a closed conformation (Calleja et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: Following growth factor stimulation, AKT shifts to an open conformation and becomes accessible to phosphorylation on threonine 308 and serine 473.
source: Following growth factor stimulation, AKT shifts to an open conformation and becomes accessible to phosphorylation on threonine 308 and serine 473, a process that requires localization of AKT to the plasma membrane through the interaction with the phospholipid products of PI3K, phosphatidyl-inositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate [PtdIns (3,4,5)P3], and PtdIns(3,4)P2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about AKT activation.

claim: AKT activation requires localization of AKT to the plasma membrane through interaction with the phospholipid products of PI3K, PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 and PtdIns(3,4)P2.
source: Following growth factor stimulation, AKT shifts to an open conformation and becomes accessible to phosphorylation on threonine 308 and serine 473, a process that requires localization of AKT to the plasma membrane through the interaction with the phospholipid products of PI3K, phosphatidyl-inositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate [PtdIns (3,4,5)P3], and PtdIns(3,4)P2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about AKT activation.

claim: Phosphorylation of AKT at T308 occurs at the plasma membrane.
source: This phosphorylation event occurs at the plasma membrane (Stephens et al., 1998) and immunofluorescence in MCF10A and EBC1 cells confirmed that kinase-dead AKT was constitutively localized to the plasma membrane (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stephens et al., 1998.

claim: R86 is a critical amino acid residue for binding of AKT to PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 and PtdIns(3,4)P2.
source: Lastly, we abolished the ability of the AKT1-K179M mutant to bind phospholipids by introducing a second substitution at an amino acid residue (R86) critical for binding of AKT to PtdIns (3,4,5)P3 and PtdIns(3,4)P2 (Thomas et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2002.

claim: R25C is a mutation known to abolish phosphoinositide binding.
source: We observed a similar result with a second mutation (R25C) known to abolish phosphoinositide binding (Thomas et al., 2002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2002.

claim: Mutations in the coding sequence of AKT are rare in human cancers.
source: Mutations in the coding sequence of AKT are rare in human cancers but provide important insights into AKT regulation (Parikh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: AKT2-G161V was found in a human melanoma sample.
source: Since AKT2-G161V was found in a human melanoma sample, we explored the pro-survival potential of this mutant in immortalized human melanocytes.
evidence: This is stated as the rationale for testing this mutant in melanocytes.

claim: Immortalized human melanocytes require TPA for survival in culture.
source: These cells required 12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol-13-acetate (TPA) for survival in culture, as has previously been reported (Arita et al., 1992), but acquired the ability to survive in TPA-deficient media (RPMI) after stable expression of AKT2-G161V (Figure 4E, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arita et al., 1992.

claim: E17K-AKT1 is the most common somatic AKT mutation in human cancer.
source: The increased PI(4,5)P2 binding of the kinase-dead G161V-AKT2 mutant (Figure 4D) was reminiscent of the most common somatic AKT mutation in human cancer (E17K-AKT1) which localizes to the plasma membrane due to increased affinity for the constitutive plasma membrane lipid PI(4,5)P2 (Carpten et al., 2007; Landgraf et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: E17K-AKT1 shows reduced sensitivity to allosteric AKT inhibitors.
source: Compared to cells transduced with wild-type AKT, cells transduced with the E17K-AKT1 mutant showed residual AKT phosphorylation at equimolar concentrations of MK2206 (Figure 4F), consistent with the reported reduced sensitivity of E17K-AKT1 to allosteric ATP kinase inhibitors (Calleja et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2010; Parikh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MFE-319 is a human endometrial cancer cell line with a kinase domain mutation in AKT1 (G311D).
source: Lastly, we identified a human endometrial cancer cell line with a kinase domain mutation in AKT1 (G311D) (Barretina et al., 2012) that failed to induce phosphorylation of endogenous AKT substrates in AKT1/2 DKO HCT116 cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Barretina et al., 2012.

claim: MK2206 is an allosteric AKT inhibitor.
source: To address this question, we compared the activity of the allosteric AKT inhibitor MK2206 (Hirai et al., 2010) with the ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors GSK690693 (Heerding et al., 2008; Rhodes et al., 2008) and GDC0068 (Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to Hirai et al., 2010.

claim: GSK690693 is an ATP-competitive AKT inhibitor.
source: To address this question, we compared the activity of the allosteric AKT inhibitor MK2206 (Hirai et al., 2010) with the ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors GSK690693 (Heerding et al., 2008; Rhodes et al., 2008) and GDC0068 (Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Heerding et al., 2008 and Rhodes et al., 2008.

claim: GDC0068 is an ATP-competitive AKT inhibitor.
source: To address this question, we compared the activity of the allosteric AKT inhibitor MK2206 (Hirai et al., 2010) with the ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors GSK690693 (Heerding et al., 2008; Rhodes et al., 2008) and GDC0068 (Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated and supported by a citation to Lin et al., 2013.

claim: Each of the AKT inhibitors (MK2206, GSK690693, GDC0068) dose dependently inhibited AKT kinase activity in EBC1 cells as determined by phosphorylation of PRAS40, GSK3β, and BAD.
source: Each of these AKT inhibitors dose dependently inhibited AKT kinase activity in the non-small-cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) cell line EBC1 as determined by phosphorylation of three AKT substrates (PRAS40, GSK3β, and BAD) in whole-cell lysates (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tryptophan 80 is a residue critical for allosteric inhibitor binding to AKT.
source: To exclude the possibility that the greater cell death induction by the allosteric AKT inhibitor was due to additional effects on proteins other than AKT, we stably expressed a synthetic AKT mutant in which a residue critical for allosteric inhibitor binding (tryptophan 80) (Green et al., 2008; Calleja et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2010) had been replaced by an alanine.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Green et al., 2008; Calleja et al., 2009; and Wu et al., 2010.

claim: Lysine 179 in AKT1 is located at the ATP-binding site.
source: To provide genetic evidence for the kinase-independent AKT function, we took advantage of a synthetic AKT mutant which is catalytically inactive due to substitution of lysine by methionine at position 179 at the ATP-binding site (AKT K179M) (Franke et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Franke et al., 1995.

claim: AKT1-K179M is catalytically inactive due to substitution of lysine by methionine at position 179 at the ATP-binding site.
source: To provide genetic evidence for the kinase-independent AKT function, we took advantage of a synthetic AKT mutant which is catalytically inactive due to substitution of lysine by methionine at position 179 at the ATP-binding site (AKT K179M) (Franke et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Franke et al., 1995.

claim: PARP cleavage is a marker of apoptosis.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed that these AKT alleles are biochemically insensitive to MK2206 and prevented the induction of PARP cleavage, a marker of apoptosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 6, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PARP cleavage.

claim: MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that mediates critical oncogenic signals through the PI3K/AKT axis.
source: We had selected EBC1 lung cancer cells for our initial studies because they harbor amplification of MET, a receptor tyrosine kinase that mediates critical oncogenic signals through the PI3K/AKT axis (Gherardi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gherardi et al., 2012.

claim: Activating EGFR mutations have been linked with aberrant PI3K pathway activation.
source: MK2206 also did not induce cell death in lung cancer cell lines with activating EGFR mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Figure 1—source data 1) which have been linked with aberrant PI3K pathway activation (Engelman et al., 2005), suggesting that the mode of PI3K activation is critical in establishing AKT addiction in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Engelman et al., 2005.

claim: ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors may induce an AKT conformation which can serve as a platform for a kinase-independent survival signal.
source: One potential explanation for our observations is that ATP-competitive AKT inhibitors might induce an AKT conformation which can serve as a platform for a kinase-independent survival signal (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: Crizotinib is a MET kinase inhibitor.
source: Despite inducing a modest amount of cell death as single agent, GSK690693 antagonized the ability of crizotinib to kill EBC1 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the context that crizotinib is used to inhibit MET in MET-amplified EBC1 cells.

claim: Protein levels of the hairpin-resistant AKT allele after doxycycline induction were similar to the levels of endogenous AKT in parental EBC1 cells.
source: Protein levels of the hairpin-resistant AKT allele after doxycycline induction were similar to the levels of endogenous AKT in parental EBC1 cells (Figure 2F, top, lanes 6 and 8 vs lanes 1 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: HCT116 cells express no endogenous AKT.
source: Consistent with a loss of membrane localization, the R86A/K179M double mutant showed loss of AKT phosphorylation at threonine 308 when expressed in HCT116 cells that express no endogenous AKT (Ericson et al., 2010) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) and it did not protect from MK2206-induced dephosphorylation in cells which do express endogenous AKT (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ericson et al., 2010.

claim: Hyper-phosphorylation of AKT in response to ATP-competitive inhibitors may be due to impaired phosphatase access.
source: It also suggests that hyper-phosphorylation of AKT in response to ATP-competitive inhibitors (Okuzumi et al., 2009) may not only be due to impaired phosphatase access (Chan et al., 2011) but also due to increased phosphorylation at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chan et al., 2011.

claim: AKT inhibitors can induce ErbB3 expression.
source: We could not explain these results by differential effects on induction of ErbB3 expression or IGF-IRβ phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 9) which can accompany AKT inhibition and mediate resistance to AKT inhibitors (Chandarlapaty et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chandarlapaty et al., 2011.

claim: ErbB3 expression and IGF-IRβ phosphorylation can accompany AKT inhibition and mediate resistance to AKT inhibitors.
source: We could not explain these results by differential effects on induction of ErbB3 expression or IGF-IRβ phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 9) which can accompany AKT inhibition and mediate resistance to AKT inhibitors (Chandarlapaty et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chandarlapaty et al., 2011.
